title: Wesley on horseback
hook: a clergyman who loved order takes to the saddle and preaches in fields to working people

segments.voice: Yesterday, Aldersgate, and a heart strangely warmed. Your line was a quarter before nine. Did you pause last night and notice what warmed your heart? Day eight hundred ninety-five.

John Wesley likes things done properly. He's a clergyman of the Church of England, trained at Oxford, and he believes preaching belongs in a church, from a pulpit, in good order. He later admits that he'd been so attached to decency and order that saving souls outside a church would once have seemed to him almost a sin. But churches are starting to close their pulpits to him. To some clergy, his preaching is too warm, too urgent. Meanwhile, outside the city, there are working people, coal miners among them, who seldom if ever set foot in a parish church. So Wesley has a choice. Today: Wesley on horseback.

He goes outside. His journal records the day he first preached in the open air, and the phrase he uses is startling: he "submitted to be more vile." He's borrowing it from King David. In Second Samuel, as the ark of God comes into Jerusalem, David dances before the LORD with all his might, and his wife Michal despises him for it. David answers, "I will yet be more vile than thus." In other words: if worship makes me look undignified, so be it. Wesley the man of order chooses to look undignified, and stands on a rise of ground in a field to preach. From then on, he travels. On horseback, year after year, along muddy roads and through all weathers, to towns, villages, mining districts, marketplaces. Tradition says he read books in the saddle, letting the horse find the way. When church officials objected that he was preaching in other men's parishes, he answered with a line from his journal: "I look upon all the world as my parish." He meant that wherever he was, he felt bound to share the good news with anyone willing to hear. The people he reached weren't gathered into a new church at first. Wesley stayed a Church of England clergyman and urged his hearers to go to their parish churches. He organized them into small groups, societies and classes, to meet and pray between Sundays, and those groups became the Methodist movement. Jesus tells a parable about a feast where the invited guests won't come, so the host sends his servant out, in the King James words, "into the highways and hedges." Wesley took the road literally.

Here's the practice: go to people where they are. In the quiet, bring to mind one person who won't come to you. Maybe they can't, maybe they won't, maybe they don't know they're welcome. A neighbor, a relative, a coworker, an old friend. Picture where they actually are today: their kitchen, their shift, their bench in the park. Breathe, and hold them there. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. If you don't, ask yourself what it would take to go to them, instead of waiting. The bell holds the time.
Methodist. The movement that grew from the small groups John Wesley organized to meet and pray between Sundays, after he took his preaching into the fields.
Your line: the world is my parish. Today, instead of waiting for someone to reach out, go to them: a call, a visit, a message that meets them where they are. Day eight hundred ninety-five.

howItsDone: Methodist churches grew from Wesley's societies and classes, and Christians in different churches still take worship outdoors, to street corners, parks and workplaces, to meet people who don't come inside.

notes: Claims rule: the index hook's 'a quarter of a million miles' was cut, and the 'hook' field reworded; no distances, sermon counts or dates are given.
Check the Wesley quotations against a public-domain edition of the Journal. The 'all the world as my parish' line comes from a letter that Wesley copied into his journal; confirm the citation.
'Tradition says he read books in the saddle': widely told; confirm or cut.
Coal miners: Wesley preached to colliers (e.g. at Kingswood near Bristol); the script keeps it general. Tomorrow's Whitefield day (897) may also feature miners; kept light here to avoid overlap.
Wesley's reluctance about field preaching is paraphrased from the journal entry where he says he could scarce reconcile himself to it; confirm.

Editor: cut 'the crowds are the wrong sort' (unsourced, sneering) and framed the objection as some clergy's view; 'never set foot' softened to 'seldom if ever'; David now dances 'before the LORD' as the ark comes into Jerusalem, as 2 Samuel 6:14–16 says.

Second editor pass: word, screen, fork and trapdoor said 'never came' to church while the hook says 'seldom if ever'; all now say 'seldom'. Michal now 'despises him', as 2 Samuel 6:16 says, rather than 'is embarrassed'.
